title: Why Was the Saturn V Painted Black and White?

scenes.text: The Saturn V is the rocket that took humans to the Moon, and it is covered in black and white stripes, like a giant barber pole. Those markings are not decoration. The rocket stood one hundred eleven meters tall, weighed almost three million kilograms, and every part of it was built for one single job, getting three people to the Moon. Today, nine parts of the Saturn V, and why each one exists.
scenes.caption: WHY BLACK AND WHITE?

scenes.text: Ten Saturn V launches carried people. Nine took astronauts to the Moon, and one stayed in Earth orbit as a test. It was a machine so large that it needed a building to be stacked in, and yet nothing on it was there by accident.
scenes.caption: NOTHING BY ACCIDENT

scenes.text: As always, every fact here comes from a named source, NASA documents and spaceflight references, all listed in the description. Let's start with the paint.
scenes.caption: WHY DOES THIS EXIST?

scenes.text: Why was the Moon rocket painted black and white? Both colors had a job. The white paint reflected the sunlight, keeping the rocket cool while it sat on the pad in the hot Florida sun. A cooler tank means less fuel boiling off, and a safer rocket. The black markings helped ground cameras measure the roll, the spin of the rocket as it rose.
scenes.query: Saturn V black and white paint
scenes.caption: WHY IS THE ROCKET BLACK AND WHITE?
scenes.short: Why Was the Saturn V Painted Black and White?

scenes.text: The early Saturn rockets had more black than the later ones. On those flights, the fuel tanks under the black areas registered heat spikes, because the dark paint absorbed the heat of the Sun. So on later Saturn V rockets, the upper black stripes and the band on the first stage were painted over in white.
scenes.query: Saturn I rocket black white stripes
scenes.caption: TOO MUCH BLACK, TOO HOT

scenes.text: So the pattern on the rocket is the result of tests. Engineers painted it, watched the temperatures, and then repainted it. It is a good reminder that even the most famous design of the century was changed by data.
scenes.caption: REPAINTED BY DATA

scenes.text: Why does the bottom of the Saturn V have five giant engines? Because the rocket had to lift almost three million kilograms off the ground. The first stage had five Rocketdyne F-1 engines, arranged in a cross with one in the middle, and together they produced about thirty-three thousand kilonewtons of thrust at sea level. That is about seven and a half million pounds.
scenes.caption: WHY DOES IT HAVE FIVE HUGE ENGINES?
scenes.short: Why Does the Saturn V Have Five Giant Engines?

scenes.text: The first stage burned for only about one hundred fifty seconds. In two and a half minutes, it used up most of its propellant, kerosene and liquid oxygen, and pushed the rocket up to the edge of space. After that, the huge stage had done all it could do, and it was dropped.
scenes.caption: 150 SECONDS OF FIRE

scenes.text: The shape of that cross matters too. One engine in the center and four around it means a layout that stays balanced, and a design in which the outer engines can be tilted to steer the rocket. It is one of the most powerful engine clusters ever flown.
scenes.caption: A CROSS OF FIRE

scenes.text: Why is there a thin tower on the very top of the rocket? It is the Launch Escape System, a rocket motor built to save the crew. If the Saturn V ever started to fail on the pad or in the first minutes, the escape rocket would pull the crew capsule up and away from the exploding rocket, and the capsule would come down on its parachutes.
scenes.query: Saturn V launch escape system tower
scenes.caption: WHY IS THERE A TOWER ON TOP?
scenes.short: Why Does the Saturn V Have a Tower on Top?
scenes.file: File:Space Center Houston Rocket Park Saturn V CSM.jpg

scenes.text: It is a rocket on top of a rocket, designed to be used only if everything goes wrong. If everything went right, it was never used. On a normal flight, it was dropped shortly after the second stage took over, because by then it was dead weight.
scenes.caption: USED ONLY IF IT ALL GOES WRONG

scenes.text: Every Apollo crew rode under that tower knowing it was there. It is a strange part, because its success is measured by never needing it. A safety system that works is one that nobody ever sees fire.
scenes.caption: A SAFETY NET YOU NEVER SEE

scenes.text: Why is there a ring between the stages? It is called the interstage, and it joins two stages that burn at different times. Its job comes at the next stage's ignition. About three minutes and twelve seconds into the flight, the interstage ring dropped away from the second stage. The ring was only about one meter from the outer engines, so it had to fall cleanly.
scenes.caption: WHY IS THERE A RING BETWEEN THE STAGES?
scenes.short: Why Does the Saturn V Have a Ring Between Its Stages?
scenes.file: File:Saturn V Rocket -- Johnson Space Center.jpg

scenes.text: The second stage engines had to light while still attached to the first stage's top, with the ring around them. When the ring dropped, the engines could burn freely, with nothing in front of the nozzles. Any problem, and the second stage could be damaged.
scenes.caption: ONE METER FROM THE FLAME

scenes.text: So a simple ring of metal had to be strong enough to hold a stage, and light enough to be dropped. And like many parts of a rocket, it worked perfectly or not at all.
scenes.caption: WORKS OR FAILS

scenes.text: What is the ring near the top of the Saturn V? It is the Instrument Unit, the rocket's brain. It sat on top of the third stage and held the guidance, navigation and control equipment. It was designed at the Marshall Space Flight Center and built by IBM. The ring is six point six meters wide and only about ninety-one centimeters tall, and it weighs about two thousand kilograms.
scenes.caption: WHAT IS THIS RING NEAR THE TOP?
scenes.short: What Is the Ring Near the Top of the Saturn V?
scenes.file: File:Saturn Instrument Unit - Evergreen Aviation & Space Museum - McMinnville, Oregon - DSC00846.jpg

scenes.text: A rocket cannot be steered by a person from the ground at that speed. So the unit measured where the rocket was, compared it to the plan, and told the engines how to point. In the end, the thing that put a spacecraft on its way to the Moon was a ring, a bit taller than a kitchen counter.
scenes.caption: THE ROCKET'S BRAIN

scenes.text: It is almost funny that so much depended on so thin a part. But a computer is mostly the volume of wires and boxes that keep it alive, and the ring was just big enough to hold them.
scenes.caption: A THIN RING, A BIG JOB

scenes.text: Why did the upper stages of the Saturn V burn a different fuel? The first stage burned kerosene, which is dense and gives a lot of push for its volume. The second and third stages burned liquid hydrogen with liquid oxygen. Hydrogen gives much more energy for each kilogram, which matters most once the rocket is high and every kilogram counts. The second stage used five J-2 engines and burned for about three hundred ninety-five seconds.
scenes.caption: WHY IS THE SECOND STAGE A DIFFERENT FUEL?
scenes.short: Why Did the Saturn V's Upper Stages Burn Hydrogen?
scenes.file: File:S-II Stage of Saturn V Rocket (67-701-c).jpeg

scenes.text: The price is the cold. Liquid hydrogen has to be kept at hundreds of degrees below zero, and it takes up a lot of room. That is why the second stage was a huge tank, nearly twenty-five meters tall, with so little else around it.
scenes.caption: A TANK OF COLD

scenes.text: So the Saturn V used the right fuel at each point of the trip. Dense fuel to leave the ground, and light, powerful fuel to go the rest of the way. Fuel was chosen the same way everything else was, for the job.
scenes.caption: THE RIGHT FUEL FOR EACH STEP

scenes.text: Why did the third stage fire two times? The first burn, about one hundred sixty-five seconds, put the spacecraft into orbit around the Earth. After a short pause, with the crew checking everything, the single J-2 engine lit a second time, for about three hundred twelve seconds, and sent them toward the Moon. This second burn is called the trans-lunar injection.
scenes.caption: WHY DID THE THIRD STAGE LIGHT TWICE?
scenes.short: Why Did the Saturn V's Third Stage Fire Twice?
scenes.file: File:Saturn V Rocket Stage S IVB - 1992.jpg

scenes.text: Starting in orbit gave the crew time to check the spacecraft before committing to the Moon. If something was wrong, they could stay near Earth. If everything was fine, the second burn took them out. It was a safe way to start a very long trip.
scenes.caption: CHECK FIRST, THEN GO

scenes.text: And after the second burn, the third stage had done its work. It stayed behind, while the crew went on in the spacecraft. The most powerful rocket ever flown by humans was, in the end, a way to push a very small capsule faster than anything had gone.
scenes.caption: A VERY SMALL PASSENGER

scenes.text: Why was the first stage so enormous? It stood forty-two meters tall and weighed about two million two hundred thousand kilograms with fuel, most of the rocket's total weight. Almost all of that was propellant. The first stage had to carry its own fuel and the weight of everything above it, and the higher the rocket went, the less it needed to carry, so most of that mass was dropped at the first stage.
scenes.query: Saturn V S-IC first stage Johnson Space Center
scenes.caption: WHY IS THE FIRST STAGE SO TALL?
scenes.short: Why Is the Saturn V's First Stage So Huge?

scenes.text: This is the basic problem of rockets. To lift fuel, you need more fuel. A rocket that carries everything to the Moon at once would be impossibly heavy. So it is built in stages, each one throwing away the part that is empty.
scenes.caption: TO LIFT FUEL YOU NEED FUEL

scenes.text: The Saturn V is the answer to that problem at its most extreme. More than ninety percent of the rocket on the pad was never going to reach the Moon. It was only there to carry the last part of it.
scenes.caption: MOST OF IT NEVER GOES

scenes.text: Why is the spacecraft so small compared to the rocket? Because it is the only part that goes to the Moon. The whole Saturn V, almost one hundred twelve meters of it, existed to move one small capsule and a lunar module. Nine of the ten crewed Saturn V flights took twenty-four astronauts to the Moon.
scenes.query: Apollo spacecraft top of Saturn V
scenes.caption: WHY IS THE SPACECRAFT SO SMALL?
scenes.short: Why Is the Apollo Spacecraft So Small Compared to the Saturn V?
scenes.file: File:Space Center Houston Rocket Park Saturn V CSM.jpg

scenes.text: Everything the astronauts needed, air, food, power and a way home, had to fit in that small space, and every kilogram of it had to be lifted by the rocket below. Engineers fought for every gram, because each gram on the capsule cost far more on the ground.
scenes.caption: EVERY GRAM COSTS KILOS

scenes.text: And that is the Saturn V in a nutshell. A tower of fuel, engines and machines, there to carry a small cone to a place that no one had been, and bring it back.
scenes.caption: A TOWER FOR A TINY CONE

scenes.text: So here are the nine. Paint that kept it cool and let cameras measure the roll, five engines in a cross, an escape tower, a ring that fell away, and a ring that was the brain. A hydrogen second stage, a third stage that lit twice, a first stage as tall as a building, and a tiny spacecraft on top.
scenes.caption: 9 PARTS. 9 REASONS.

scenes.text: Next time you see the black and white rocket in a museum, you will know that every stripe and every ring is there for a reason. If you want more machines explained part by part, subscribe to Machine Reverse. And tell us in the comments which machine you want us to take apart next.
